issues.legal_issue: A mining suspension may be lifted only for a leaseholder with a subsisting legal right to mine, in addition to the required operational clearances.
material_facts: Mining operations had been suspended because the leaseholders lacked required clearances, approvals or consent.
Leaseholders later sought to lift the suspension on the basis that they had obtained the required clearances.
The Court held that clearances could support renewed operations only if the leaseholder also had a subsisting mining lease.
issues.conclusion: A subsisting mining lease is a necessary precondition to lifting the suspension; obtaining clearances alone does not establish a right to resume mining.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, mining cannot be carried on without a valid, subsisting lease. A lease subsists while its original grant or a valid renewal remains in force, or where a statutory deemed extension applies. The order suspending operations for lack of clearances did not dispense with the requirement that the lease itself subsist.

predicates.suspension_lifting_application: A leaseholder applied to have a court-imposed suspension of mining operations lifted.
predicates.lease_right_not_subsisting: The leaseholder did not have a valid, subsisting legal right to carry on mining operations.

issues.definition: When a leaseholder applies to lift a mining suspension but lacks a subsisting right to mine, the suspension cannot be lifted.

issues.legal_issue: A timely, undecided application for the first renewal of a mining lease can result in a deemed extension, but that extension is limited by the governing renewal rules.
material_facts: The applicable version of Rule 24A(6) deemed a lease extended when a timely renewal application had not been decided before the lease expired.
The Court interpreted the earlier and amended versions of the rule together and accepted that the deemed-extension benefit applied to first renewals.
The amended rule provided a limited further extension for qualifying first-renewal applications that remained pending.
issues.conclusion: A leaseholder with a timely, undecided application for a first renewal may rely on the applicable deemed-extension regime; the extension is not unlimited.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 24A(1) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 required a renewal application to be made at least twelve months before expiry. The former Rule 24A(6) deemed an eligible lease extended until the State Government decided the application; the amended Rule 24A(6) limited the extension and specified treatment for pending first-renewal applications. The Court read the provisions in sequence and applied them to first renewals.

predicates.lease_extension_dispute: A court proceeding concerned whether a mining lease continued after its stated expiry.
predicates.timely_first_renewal_application: The leaseholder applied for the first renewal sufficiently before the existing lease was due to expire.
predicates.first_renewal_application_undecided: The first-renewal application had not been rejected or finally decided.

issues.definition: In a lease-extension dispute, a timely first-renewal application that remains undecided permits the leaseholder to receive the deemed extension available under the applicable rules.

issues.legal_issue: A second or later renewal does not arise by deemed extension and requires an express renewal order.
material_facts: Some leaseholders relied on pending applications for second or later renewals to claim that their leases continued.
A second or later renewal under the applicable statutory scheme required the State Government to record reasons that renewal was in the interest of mineral development.
The applicable rules did not provide deemed extension for those renewals, and the statute also required prior Central Government approval.
issues.conclusion: A pending application for a second or later renewal does not itself continue the lease; continuation requires an express renewal order meeting the applicable requirements.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 made a second or later renewal dependent on the State Government forming and recording the required opinion, while Section 8(4) required prior Central Government approval for the specified minerals. Rule 24A(6) did not supply a deemed extension for such renewals. In Goa Foundation v. Union of India, the Court held that deemed extension could not replace the express decision required for a renewal under Section 8(3). The Court also referred to TISCO Ltd. v. Union of India for the principle that the statutory conditions for further renewal must be followed strictly.

rule.if: lease_extension_dispute and subsequent_renewal_application and not express_subsequent_renewal_order

predicates.lease_extension_dispute: A court proceeding concerned whether a mining lease continued after its stated expiry.
predicates.subsequent_renewal_application: The leaseholder applied for a second or later renewal of the mining lease.
predicates.express_subsequent_renewal_order: The competent government issued an express order granting the second or later renewal.

issues.definition: In a lease-extension dispute, a pending application for a second or later renewal without an express grant does not create a deemed renewal.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory extension regime for pre-amendment mining leases can apply even when the lease or its renewal expired before the amendment, if a valid renewal application remained undecided and the lease conditions were met.
material_facts: The parties disputed whether the amended statutory extension regime covered only leases subsisting when the amendment commenced.
Some leaseholders had made renewal applications at least twelve months before expiry, and those applications remained undecided.
The Court held that expiry of the grant or renewal was not, by itself, rejection, determination or lapse within the statutory exclusion.
The Court made entitlement subject to compliance with all lease terms and conditions, including required clearances and approvals.
issues.conclusion: The amended extension regime can benefit a leaseholder whose lease or renewal had expired before the amendment if a valid, timely renewal application remained undecided and the lease conditions were complied with; leases rejected, determined or lapsed are excluded.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 8A(5), 8A(6) and 8A(9) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 provide extensions for qualifying pre-amendment leases and exclude leases whose renewal was rejected, which were determined, or which lapsed. The Court treated those terms as distinct from mere expiry. It relied on the statutory text and the amendment's Objects and Reasons, which addressed pending renewal applications and hardship caused by administrative delay. Extension remained subject to compliance with all lease terms and conditions.

rule.if: lease_extension_dispute and pre_amendment_lease_expired and timely_renewal_application_pending and lease_terms_complied and lease_not_rejected_determined_or_lapsed

predicates.lease_extension_dispute: A court proceeding concerned the continued validity or extension of a mining lease.
predicates.pre_amendment_lease_expired: A mining lease granted before a statutory change had expired before that change took effect.
predicates.timely_renewal_application_pending: The leaseholder had applied for renewal sufficiently before expiry and the application remained undecided.
predicates.lease_terms_complied: The leaseholder had complied with the applicable terms and conditions of the lease, including required operational clearances and approvals.
predicates.lease_not_rejected_determined_or_lapsed: The renewal had not been rejected and the lease had not been formally brought to an end or lapsed under the applicable process.

issues.definition: For an expired pre-change lease, a timely pending renewal application and compliance with lease conditions permit the amended extension regime to apply, unless the lease has been rejected, determined or lapsed.

issues.legal_issue: For qualifying renewed leases, the applicable extension is the one that preserves the lease for the longest period among the statutory alternatives.
material_facts: The amended statute addressed pre-amendment leases used for captive and non-captive purposes and provided different end points for each category.
It provided alternatives based on the last renewal's expiry, the period already granted by a renewal, and treating the original grant as having a fifty-year term.
The Court held that the alternative extending the lease period farthest would benefit the leaseholder.
issues.conclusion: The leaseholder receives the longest of the applicable statutory extensions, subject to compliance with the lease conditions.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 8A(5) and 8A(6) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 set out three relevant extension contingencies for qualifying pre-amendment leases: extension to the applicable statutory end point after an expired renewal, preservation of a renewal that runs beyond that end point, and the benefit of treating the original grant as having a fifty-year term. The Court held that the contingency extending the lease farthest governs, subject to compliance with the lease terms and conditions.

predicates.lease_extension_dispute: A court proceeding concerned the continued validity or extension of a mining lease.
predicates.qualifying_pre_amendment_renewed_lease: The mining lease was granted before the statutory change and had been extended or was subject to a renewal covered by the extension regime.
predicates.lease_terms_complied: The leaseholder had complied with the applicable terms and conditions of the lease.

issues.definition: For a qualifying pre-change renewed lease whose conditions are met, the applicable statutory alternative that extends the lease farthest controls.

issues.legal_issue: A mining lease does not lapse automatically for inactivity; lapse requires a government order declaring it and communicating that declaration to the leaseholder.
material_facts: The statute provided that a lease could lapse after a continuous period without mining operations.
Rule 28(1) required the State Government to declare the lease lapsed by order and communicate that declaration to the lessee.
The Court rejected the argument that the lapse occurred automatically upon the period of inactivity ending.
issues.conclusion: Inactivity alone does not establish that the lease has lapsed; the State Government must issue and communicate an order declaring lapse.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4A(4) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 addresses lapse for failure to commence or continuation of mining operations. Read with Rule 28(1) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, it requires a State Government order declaring lapse and communication of that declaration to the leaseholder. The Court concluded that lapse is not automatic.

rule.if: lease_lapse_dispute and inactivity_lapse_condition_met and not lapse_order_communicated

predicates.lease_lapse_dispute: A court proceeding concerned whether a mining lease had lapsed because of inactivity.
predicates.inactivity_lapse_condition_met: The leaseholder had failed to commence mining operations or had discontinued them for the prescribed continuous period.
predicates.lapse_order_communicated: The State Government had issued an order declaring the lease lapsed and communicated it to the leaseholder.

issues.definition: In a lapse dispute, meeting the inactivity condition without a communicated government lapse order means the lease has not yet lapsed.

issues.legal_issue: A timely application seeking continuation of a lease because mining operations could not be conducted prevents lapse while the application awaits decision, subject to the prescribed limit.
material_facts: Rule 28 allowed a leaseholder to apply for continuation where mining operations could not be commenced or had been discontinued for reasons beyond the leaseholder's control.

Rule 28(4) provided that if the State Government did not decide the application before the lease would otherwise lapse, the lease was deemed extended until the decision or the prescribed outer limit, whichever came first.
The Court relied on that provision in rejecting the claim that lapse was automatic.
issues.conclusion: When such an application is pending, the lease is deemed to continue during the period specified by the rule, unless and until the applicable limit is reached.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 28(2) and Rule 28(4) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 permit an application for relief from lapse and deem the lease extended if the State Government has not decided the application by the date it would otherwise lapse. The deemed continuation lasts until the State Government decides the application or the prescribed outer limit is reached, whichever occurs first.

predicates.lease_lapse_dispute: A court proceeding concerned whether a mining lease had lapsed because operations had not commenced or had been discontinued.
predicates.timely_lapse_relief_application: The leaseholder applied within the required time for relief from lapse based on reasons beyond the leaseholder's control.
predicates.application_undecided: The State Government had not yet decided the application for relief from lapse.

issues.definition: In a lapse dispute, a timely undecided application for relief means the lease is deemed to continue while the application is pending, subject to the applicable limit.
